 388 |     def add_edges(self, G, graph_element):
 389 |         def edge_key_data(G):

 391 |             if G.is_multigraph():

 393 |                     edge_data = data.copy()

 396 |                     if edge_id is None:
 397 |                         edge_id = next(self.edge_id)
 398 |                         while str(edge_id) in self.all_edge_ids:
 399 |                             edge_id = next(self.edge_id)
 400 |                         self.all_edge_ids.add(str(edge_id))
 401 |                     yield u, v, edge_id, edge_data
 402 |             else:
 403 |                 for u, v, data in G.edges(data=True):
 404 |                     edge_data = data.copy()

 408 |                         while str(edge_id) in self.all_edge_ids:
 409 |                             edge_id = next(self.edge_id)
 410 |                         self.all_edge_ids.add(str(edge_id))
 411 |                     yield u, v, edge_id, edge_data
 412 | 
 413 |         edges_element = Element("edges")
 414 |         for u, v, key, edge_data in edge_key_data(G):
 415 |             kw = {"id": str(key)}
 416 |             try:
 417 |                 edge_label = edge_data.pop("label")

 442 |                 pass
 443 |             source_id = str(G.nodes[u].get("id", u))
 444 |             target_id = str(G.nodes[v].get("id", v))
 445 |             edge_element = Element("edge", source=source_id, target=target_id, **kw)

 460 |     def add_attributes(self, node_or_edge, xml_obj, data, default):
 461 |         # Add attrvalues to node or edge
 462 |         attvalues = Element("attvalues")
 463 |         if len(data) == 0:
 464 |             return data
 465 |         mode = "static"
 466 |         for k, v in data.items():
 467 |             # rename generic multigraph key to avoid any name conflict
 468 |             if k == "key":
 469 |                 k = "networkx_key"
 470 |             val_type = type(v)
 471 |             if val_type not in self.xml_type:
 472 |                 raise TypeError(f"attribute value type is not allowed: {val_type}")
 473 |             if isinstance(v, list):
 474 |                 # dynamic data
 475 |                 for val, start, end in v:
 476 |                     val_type = type(val)
 477 |                     if start is not None or end is not None:
 478 |                         mode = "dynamic"
 479 |                         self.alter_graph_mode_timeformat(start)
 480 |                         self.alter_graph_mode_timeformat(end)
 481 |                         break
 482 |                 attr_id = self.get_attr_id(
 483 |                     str(k), self.xml_type[val_type], node_or_edge, default, mode
 484 |                 )
 485 |                 for val, start, end in v:
 486 |                     e = Element("attvalue")
 487 |                     e.attrib["for"] = attr_id
 488 |                     e.attrib["value"] = str(val)
 489 |                     # Handle nan, inf, -inf differently
 490 |                     if val_type == float:
 491 |                         if e.attrib["value"] == "inf":
 492 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "INF"
 493 |                         elif e.attrib["value"] == "nan":
 494 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "NaN"
 495 |                         elif e.attrib["value"] == "-inf":
 496 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "-INF"
 497 |                     if start is not None:
 498 |                         e.attrib["start"] = str(start)
 499 |                     if end is not None:
 500 |                         e.attrib["end"] = str(end)
 501 |                     attvalues.append(e)
 502 |             else:
 503 |                 # static data
 504 |                 mode = "static"
 505 |                 attr_id = self.get_attr_id(
 506 |                     str(k), self.xml_type[val_type], node_or_edge, default, mode
 507 |                 )
 508 |                 e = Element("attvalue")
 509 |                 e.attrib["for"] = attr_id
 510 |                 if isinstance(v, bool):

 512 |                 else:
 513 |                     e.attrib["value"] = str(v)
 514 |                     # Handle float nan, inf, -inf differently

 516 |                         if e.attrib["value"] == "inf":

 518 |                         elif e.attrib["value"] == "nan":

 521 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "-INF"
 522 |                 attvalues.append(e)

 526 |     def get_attr_id(self, title, attr_type, edge_or_node, default, mode):
 527 |         # find the id of the attribute or generate a new id
 528 |         try:
 529 |             return self.attr[edge_or_node][mode][title]
 530 |         except KeyError:
 531 |             # generate new id
 532 |             new_id = str(next(self.attr_id))
 533 |             self.attr[edge_or_node][mode][title] = new_id
 534 |             attr_kwargs = {"id": new_id, "title": title, "type": attr_type}
 535 |             attribute = Element("attribute", **attr_kwargs)
 536 |             # add subelement for data default value if present
 537 |             default_title = default.get(title)
 538 |             if default_title is not None:
 539 |                 default_element = Element("default")
 540 |                 default_element.text = str(default_title)
 541 |                 attribute.append(default_element)
 542 |             # new insert it into the XML
 543 |             attributes_element = None
 544 |             for a in self.graph_element.findall("attributes"):
 545 |                 # find existing attributes element by class and mode
 546 |                 a_class = a.get("class")
 547 |                 a_mode = a.get("mode", "static")
 548 |                 if a_class == edge_or_node and a_mode == mode:
 549 |                     attributes_element = a
 550 |             if attributes_element is None:
 551 |                 # create new attributes element
 552 |                 attr_kwargs = {"mode": mode, "class": edge_or_node}
 553 |                 attributes_element = Element("attributes", **attr_kwargs)
 554 |                 self.graph_element.insert(0, attributes_element)
 555 |             attributes_element.append(attribute)

 679 |             if not elem.tail or not elem.tail.strip():

 713 |     def make_graph(self, graph_xml):
 714 |         # start with empty DiGraph or MultiDiGraph
 715 |         edgedefault = graph_xml.get("defaultedgetype", None)
 716 |         if edgedefault == "directed":
 717 |             G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
 718 |         else:
 719 |             G = nx.MultiGraph()
 720 | 
 721 |         # graph attributes
 722 |         graph_name = graph_xml.get("name", "")
 723 |         if graph_name != "":
 724 |             G.graph["name"] = graph_name
 725 |         graph_start = graph_xml.get("start")
 726 |         if graph_start is not None:
 727 |             G.graph["start"] = graph_start
 728 |         graph_end = graph_xml.get("end")
 729 |         if graph_end is not None:
 730 |             G.graph["end"] = graph_end
 731 |         graph_mode = graph_xml.get("mode", "")
 732 |         if graph_mode == "dynamic":
 733 |             G.graph["mode"] = "dynamic"
 734 |         else:
 735 |             G.graph["mode"] = "static"
 736 | 
 737 |         # timeformat
 738 |         self.timeformat = graph_xml.get("timeformat")
 739 |         if self.timeformat == "date":
 740 |             self.timeformat = "string"
 741 | 
 742 |         # node and edge attributes
 743 |         attributes_elements = graph_xml.findall(f"{{{self.NS_GEXF}}}attributes")
 744 |         # dictionaries to hold attributes and attribute defaults
 745 |         node_attr = {}
 746 |         node_default = {}
 747 |         edge_attr = {}
 748 |         edge_default = {}
 749 |         for a in attributes_elements:
 750 |             attr_class = a.get("class")
 751 |             if attr_class == "node":
 752 |                 na, nd = self.find_gexf_attributes(a)
 753 |                 node_attr.update(na)

 755 |                 G.graph["node_default"] = node_default
 756 |             elif attr_class == "edge":

 762 |                 raise  # unknown attribute class

 767 |         ed = {}

 769 |         edge_default.update(ed)

 771 | 
 772 |         # add nodes

 774 |         if nodes_element is not None:
 775 |             for node_xml in nodes_element.findall(f"{{{self.NS_GEXF}}}node"):

 388 |     def add_edges(self, G, graph_element):

 397 |                         edge_id = next(self.edge_id)

 399 |                             edge_id = next(self.edge_id)
 400 |                         self.all_edge_ids.add(str(edge_id))
 401 |                     yield u, v, edge_id, edge_data
 402 |             else:
 403 |                 for u, v, data in G.edges(data=True):
 404 |                     edge_data = data.copy()

 409 |                             edge_id = next(self.edge_id)
 410 |                         self.all_edge_ids.add(str(edge_id))
 411 |                     yield u, v, edge_id, edge_data

 415 |             kw = {"id": str(key)}
 416 |             try:
 417 |                 edge_label = edge_data.pop("label")

 442 |                 pass

 460 |     def add_attributes(self, node_or_edge, xml_obj, data, default):
 461 |         # Add attrvalues to node or edge
 462 |         attvalues = Element("attvalues")
 463 |         if len(data) == 0:
 464 |             return data
 465 |         mode = "static"
 466 |         for k, v in data.items():
 467 |             # rename generic multigraph key to avoid any name conflict
 468 |             if k == "key":
 469 |                 k = "networkx_key"
 470 |             val_type = type(v)
 471 |             if val_type not in self.xml_type:
 472 |                 raise TypeError(f"attribute value type is not allowed: {val_type}")
 473 |             if isinstance(v, list):
 474 |                 # dynamic data
 475 |                 for val, start, end in v:
 476 |                     val_type = type(val)
 477 |                     if start is not None or end is not None:
 478 |                         mode = "dynamic"
 479 |                         self.alter_graph_mode_timeformat(start)
 480 |                         self.alter_graph_mode_timeformat(end)

 482 |                 attr_id = self.get_attr_id(
 483 |                     str(k), self.xml_type[val_type], node_or_edge, default, mode
 484 |                 )
 485 |                 for val, start, end in v:
 486 |                     e = Element("attvalue")
 487 |                     e.attrib["for"] = attr_id
 488 |                     e.attrib["value"] = str(val)
 489 |                     # Handle nan, inf, -inf differently
 490 |                     if val_type == float:
 491 |                         if e.attrib["value"] == "inf":
 492 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "INF"
 493 |                         elif e.attrib["value"] == "nan":
 494 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "NaN"
 495 |                         elif e.attrib["value"] == "-inf":
 496 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "-INF"
 497 |                     if start is not None:
 498 |                         e.attrib["start"] = str(start)
 499 |                     if end is not None:
 500 |                         e.attrib["end"] = str(end)
 501 |                     attvalues.append(e)
 502 |             else:
 503 |                 # static data
 504 |                 mode = "static"
 505 |                 attr_id = self.get_attr_id(
 506 |                     str(k), self.xml_type[val_type], node_or_edge, default, mode
 507 |                 )
 508 |                 e = Element("attvalue")
 509 |                 e.attrib["for"] = attr_id
 510 |                 if isinstance(v, bool):

 512 |                 else:
 513 |                     e.attrib["value"] = str(v)
 514 |                     # Handle float nan, inf, -inf differently

 521 |                             e.attrib["value"] = "-INF"
 522 |                 attvalues.append(e)

 526 |     def get_attr_id(self, title, attr_type, edge_or_node, default, mode):
 527 |         # find the id of the attribute or generate a new id
 528 |         try:
 529 |             return self.attr[edge_or_node][mode][title]
 530 |         except KeyError:
 531 |             # generate new id
 532 |             new_id = str(next(self.attr_id))
 533 |             self.attr[edge_or_node][mode][title] = new_id
 534 |             attr_kwargs = {"id": new_id, "title": title, "type": attr_type}
 535 |             attribute = Element("attribute", **attr_kwargs)
 536 |             # add subelement for data default value if present
 537 |             default_title = default.get(title)
 538 |             if default_title is not None:
 539 |                 default_element = Element("default")
 540 |                 default_element.text = str(default_title)
 541 |                 attribute.append(default_element)
 542 |             # new insert it into the XML
 543 |             attributes_element = None
 544 |             for a in self.graph_element.findall("attributes"):
 545 |                 # find existing attributes element by class and mode
 546 |                 a_class = a.get("class")
 547 |                 a_mode = a.get("mode", "static")
 548 |                 if a_class == edge_or_node and a_mode == mode:
 549 |                     attributes_element = a

 553 |                 attributes_element = Element("attributes", **attr_kwargs)
 554 |                 self.graph_element.insert(0, attributes_element)
 555 |             attributes_element.append(attribute)

 679 |             if not elem.tail or not elem.tail.strip():

 713 |     def make_graph(self, graph_xml):
 714 |         # start with empty DiGraph or MultiDiGraph
 715 |         edgedefault = graph_xml.get("defaultedgetype", None)
 716 |         if edgedefault == "directed":
 717 |             G = nx.MultiDiGraph()
 718 |         else:
 719 |             G = nx.MultiGraph()

 721 |         # graph attributes
 722 |         graph_name = graph_xml.get("name", "")
 723 |         if graph_name != "":
 724 |             G.graph["name"] = graph_name
 725 |         graph_start = graph_xml.get("start")
 726 |         if graph_start is not None:
 727 |             G.graph["start"] = graph_start
 728 |         graph_end = graph_xml.get("end")
 729 |         if graph_end is not None:
 730 |             G.graph["end"] = graph_end
 731 |         graph_mode = graph_xml.get("mode", "")
 732 |         if graph_mode == "dynamic":
 733 |             G.graph["mode"] = "dynamic"
 734 |         else:
 735 |             G.graph["mode"] = "static"
 736 | 
 737 |         # timeformat
 738 |         self.timeformat = graph_xml.get("timeformat")
 739 |         if self.timeformat == "date":
 740 |             self.timeformat = "string"
 741 | 
 742 |         # node and edge attributes

 744 |         # dictionaries to hold attributes and attribute defaults
 745 |         node_attr = {}

 748 |         edge_default = {}
 749 |         for a in attributes_elements:

 774 |         if nodes_element is not None:

 717 | # Handle ANSI escape sequences for both control sequence introducer (CSI) and
 718 | # operating system command (OSC). Both of these begin with 0x1b (or octal 033),
 719 | # which will be shown below as ESC.
 720 | #
 721 | # CSI ANSI escape codes have the following format, defined in section 5.4 of ECMA-48:
 722 | #
 723 | # CSI: ESC followed by the '[' character (0x5b)
 724 | # Parameter Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x30-0x3f
 725 | # Intermediate Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x20-0x2f
 726 | # Final Byte: a single byte in the range 0x40-0x7e
 727 | #
 728 | # Also include the terminal hyperlink sequences as described here:
 729 | # https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda
 730 | #
 731 | # OSC 8 ; params ; uri ST display_text OSC 8 ;; ST
 732 | #
 733 | # Example: \x1b]8;;https://example.com\x5ctext to show\x1b]8;;\x5c
 734 | #
 735 | # Where:
 736 | # OSC: ESC followed by the ']' character (0x5d)
 737 | # params: 0..n optional key value pairs separated by ':' (e.g. foo=bar:baz=qux:abc=123)
 738 | # URI: the actual URI with protocol scheme (e.g. https://, file://, ftp://)
 739 | # ST: ESC followed by the '\' character (0x5c)
 740 | _esc = r"\x1b"
 741 | _csi = rf"{_esc}\["
 742 | _osc = rf"{_esc}\]"
 743 | _st = rf"{_esc}\\"
 744 | 
 745 | _ansi_escape_pat = rf"""
 746 |     (
 747 |         # terminal colors, etc
 748 |         {_csi}        # CSI
 749 |         [\x30-\x3f]*  # parameter bytes
 750 |         [\x20-\x2f]*  # intermediate bytes
 751 |         [\x40-\x7e]   # final byte
 752 |     |
 753 |         # terminal hyperlinks
 754 |         {_osc}8;        # OSC opening
 755 |         (\w+=\w+:?)*    # key=value params list (submatch 2)
 756 |         ;               # delimiter
 757 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # URI - anything but ESC (submatch 3)
 758 |         {_st}           # ST
 759 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # link text - anything but ESC (submatch 4)
 760 |         {_osc}8;;{_st}  # "closing" OSC sequence
 761 |     )
 762 | """
 763 | _ansi_codes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat, re.VERBOSE)
 764 | _ansi_codes_bytes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat.encode("utf8"), re.VERBOSE)

 792 | def _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 793 |     """
 794 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".")
 795 |     False
 796 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1")
 797 |     True
 798 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1.")
 799 |     True
 800 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".1")
 801 |     True
 802 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1000")
 803 |     False
 804 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000")
 805 |     True
 806 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,0000")
 807 |     False
 808 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000.1234")
 809 |     True
 810 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(b"1,000.1234")
 811 |     True
 812 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("+1,000.1234")
 813 |     True
 814 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("-1,000.1234")
 815 |     True
 816 |     """
 817 |     try:
 818 |         string = string.decode()
 819 |     except (UnicodeDecodeError, AttributeError):
 820 |         pass

 833 | def _isnumber(string):
 834 |     """
 835 |     >>> _isnumber("123.45")
 836 |     True
 837 |     >>> _isnumber("123")
 838 |     True
 839 |     >>> _isnumber("spam")
 840 |     False
 841 |     >>> _isnumber("123e45678")
 842 |     False
 843 |     >>> _isnumber("inf")
 844 |     True
 845 |     """
 846 |     if not _isconvertible(float, string):
 847 |         return False
 848 |     elif isinstance(string, (str, bytes)) and (
 849 |         math.isinf(float(string)) or math.isnan(float(string))
 850 |     ):
 851 |         return string.lower() in ["inf", "-inf", "nan"]
 852 |     return True

 883 | def _type(string, has_invisible=True, numparse=True):
 884 |     """The least generic type (type(None), int, float, str, unicode).
 885 | 
 886 |     >>> _type(None) is type(None)
 887 |     True

 889 |     True
 890 |     >>> _type("1") is type(1)
 891 |     True
 892 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 893 |     True
 894 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 895 |     True
 896 | 
 897 |     """
 898 | 
 899 |     if has_invisible and isinstance(string, (str, bytes)):
 900 |         string = _strip_ansi(string)
 901 |

 903 |         return type(None)
 904 |     elif hasattr(string, "isoformat"):  # datetime.datetime, date, and time
 905 |         return str
 906 |     elif _isbool(string):
 907 |         return bool
 908 |     elif _isint(string) and numparse:
 909 |         return int
 910 |     elif _isnumber(string) and numparse:
 911 |         return float
 912 |     elif isinstance(string, bytes):

 918 | def _afterpoint(string):
 919 |     """Symbols after a decimal point, -1 if the string lacks the decimal point.
 920 | 
 921 |     >>> _afterpoint("123.45")
 922 |     2
 923 |     >>> _afterpoint("1001")
 924 |     -1
 925 |     >>> _afterpoint("eggs")
 926 |     -1
 927 |     >>> _afterpoint("123e45")
 928 |     2
 929 |     >>> _afterpoint("123,456.78")
 930 |     2
 931 | 
 932 |     """
 933 |     if _isnumber(string) or _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 934 |         if _isint(string):
 935 |             return -1
 936 |         else:
 937 |             pos = string.rfind(".")
 938 |             pos = string.lower().rfind("e") if pos < 0 else pos
 939 |             if pos >= 0:
 940 |                 return len(string) - pos - 1
 941 |             else:
 942 |                 return -1  # no point
 943 |     else:
 944 |         return -1  # not a number

 991 |     >>> repr(_strip_ansi('\x1B]8;;https://example.com\x1B\\This is a link\x1B]8;;\x1B\\'))
 992 |     "'This is a link'"

1566 |     colalign=None,
1567 |     maxcolwidths=None,
1568 |     rowalign=None,
1569 |     maxheadercolwidths=None,
1570 | ):
1571 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1572 | 
1573 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1574 |     ---  ---------
1575 |       1      2.34
1576 |     -56      8.999
1577 |       2  10001
1578 |     ---  ---------
1579 | 
1580 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1581 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1582 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1583 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1584 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1585 | 
1586 | 
1587 |     Table headers
1588 |     -------------
1589 | 
1590 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1591 | 
1592 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1593 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1594 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1595 | 
1596 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1597 | 
1598 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1599 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1600 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1601 | 
1602 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1603 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1604 |            sex      age
1605 |     -----  -----  -----
1606 |     Alice  F         24
1607 |     Bob    M         19
1608 | 
1609 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1610 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1611 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1612 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1613 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1614 | 
1615 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1616 |     -  -  --
1617 |     0  F  24
1618 |     1  M  19
1619 |     -  -  --
1620 | 
1621 | 
1622 |     Column alignment
1623 |     ----------------
1624 | 
1625 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1626 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1627 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1628 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1629 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1630 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1631 | 
1632 | 
1633 |     Table formats
1634 |     -------------
1635 | 
1636 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1637 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1638 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1639 | 
1640 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1641 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1642 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1643 | 
1644 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1645 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1646 |     columns):
1647 | 
1648 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1649 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1650 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1651 |     -----  --  ----
1652 |     spam    1  ?
1653 |     eggs   42  3.14
1654 |     other   ?  2.7
1655 |     -----  --  ----

1657 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:

1660 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.

2007 |     Number parsing
2008 |     --------------
2009 |     By default, anything which can be parsed as a number is a number.
2010 |     This ensures numbers represented as strings are aligned properly.
2011 |     This can lead to weird results for particular strings such as
2012 |     specific git SHAs e.g. "42992e1" will be parsed into the number
2013 |     429920 and aligned as such.
2014 | 
2015 |     To completely disable number parsing (and alignment), use
2016 |     `disable_numparse=True`. For more fine grained control, a list column
2017 |     indices is used to disable number parsing only on those columns
2018 |     e.g. `disable_numparse=[0, 2]` would disable number parsing only on the
2019 |     first and third columns.
2020 | 
2021 |     Column Widths and Auto Line Wrapping
2022 |     ------------------------------------
2023 |     Tabulate will, by default, set the width of each column to the length of the
2024 |     longest element in that column. However, in situations where fields are expected
2025 |     to reasonably be too long to look good as a single line, tabulate can help automate
2026 |     word wrapping long fields for you. Use the parameter `maxcolwidth` to provide a
2027 |     list of maximal column widths
2028 | 
2029 |     >>> print(tabulate( \
2030 |           [('1', 'John Smith', \
2031 |             'This is a rather long description that might look better if it is wrapped a bit')], \
2032 |           headers=("Issue Id", "Author", "Description"), \
2033 |           maxcolwidths=[None, None, 30], \
2034 |           tablefmt="grid"  \
2035 |         ))
2036 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2037 |     |   Issue Id | Author     | Description                   |
2038 |     +============+============+===============================+
2039 |     |          1 | John Smith | This is a rather long         |
2040 |     |            |            | description that might look   |
2041 |     |            |            | better if it is wrapped a bit |
2042 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2043 | 
2044 |     Header column width can be specified in a similar way using `maxheadercolwidth`
2045 | 
2046 |     """
2047 | 
2048 |     if tabular_data is None:
2049 |         tabular_data = []
2050 | 
2051 |     list_of_lists, headers = _normalize_tabular_data(
2052 |         tabular_data, headers, showindex=showindex
2053 |     )
2054 |     list_of_lists, separating_lines = _remove_separating_lines(list_of_lists)
2055 | 
2056 |     if maxcolwidths is not None:
2057 |         num_cols = len(list_of_lists[0])
2058 |         if isinstance(maxcolwidths, int):  # Expand scalar for all columns
2059 |             maxcolwidths = _expand_iterable(maxcolwidths, num_cols, maxcolwidths)
2060 |         else:  # Ignore col width for any 'trailing' columns
2061 |             maxcolwidths = _expand_iterable(maxcolwidths, num_cols, None)
2062 | 
2063 |         numparses = _expand_numparse(disable_numparse, num_cols)
2064 |         list_of_lists = _wrap_text_to_colwidths(
2065 |             list_of_lists, maxcolwidths, numparses=numparses
2066 |         )
2067 |

 717 | # Handle ANSI escape sequences for both control sequence introducer (CSI) and
 718 | # operating system command (OSC). Both of these begin with 0x1b (or octal 033),
 719 | # which will be shown below as ESC.
 720 | #
 721 | # CSI ANSI escape codes have the following format, defined in section 5.4 of ECMA-48:
 722 | #
 723 | # CSI: ESC followed by the '[' character (0x5b)
 724 | # Parameter Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x30-0x3f
 725 | # Intermediate Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x20-0x2f
 726 | # Final Byte: a single byte in the range 0x40-0x7e
 727 | #
 728 | # Also include the terminal hyperlink sequences as described here:
 729 | # https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda
 730 | #
 731 | # OSC 8 ; params ; uri ST display_text OSC 8 ;; ST
 732 | #
 733 | # Example: \x1b]8;;https://example.com\x5ctext to show\x1b]8;;\x5c
 734 | #
 735 | # Where:
 736 | # OSC: ESC followed by the ']' character (0x5d)
 737 | # params: 0..n optional key value pairs separated by ':' (e.g. foo=bar:baz=qux:abc=123)
 738 | # URI: the actual URI with protocol scheme (e.g. https://, file://, ftp://)
 739 | # ST: ESC followed by the '\' character (0x5c)
 740 | _esc = r"\x1b"
 741 | _csi = rf"{_esc}\["
 742 | _osc = rf"{_esc}\]"
 743 | _st = rf"{_esc}\\"
 744 | 
 745 | _ansi_escape_pat = rf"""
 746 |     (
 747 |         # terminal colors, etc
 748 |         {_csi}        # CSI
 749 |         [\x30-\x3f]*  # parameter bytes
 750 |         [\x20-\x2f]*  # intermediate bytes
 751 |         [\x40-\x7e]   # final byte
 752 |     |
 753 |         # terminal hyperlinks
 754 |         {_osc}8;        # OSC opening
 755 |         (\w+=\w+:?)*    # key=value params list (submatch 2)
 756 |         ;               # delimiter
 757 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # URI - anything but ESC (submatch 3)
 758 |         {_st}           # ST
 759 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # link text - anything but ESC (submatch 4)
 760 |         {_osc}8;;{_st}  # "closing" OSC sequence
 761 |     )
 762 | """
 763 | _ansi_codes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat, re.VERBOSE)
 764 | _ansi_codes_bytes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat.encode("utf8"), re.VERBOSE)

 792 | def _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 793 |     """
 794 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".")
 795 |     False
 796 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1")
 797 |     True
 798 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1.")
 799 |     True
 800 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".1")
 801 |     True
 802 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1000")
 803 |     False
 804 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000")
 805 |     True
 806 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,0000")
 807 |     False
 808 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000.1234")
 809 |     True
 810 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(b"1,000.1234")
 811 |     True
 812 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("+1,000.1234")
 813 |     True
 814 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("-1,000.1234")
 815 |     True
 816 |     """
 817 |     try:
 818 |         string = string.decode()
 819 |     except (UnicodeDecodeError, AttributeError):
 820 |         pass
 821 | 
 822 |     return bool(re.match(_float_with_thousands_separators, string))

 833 | def _isnumber(string):
 834 |     """
 835 |     >>> _isnumber("123.45")
 836 |     True
 837 |     >>> _isnumber("123")
 838 |     True
 839 |     >>> _isnumber("spam")
 840 |     False
 841 |     >>> _isnumber("123e45678")
 842 |     False
 843 |     >>> _isnumber("inf")
 844 |     True
 845 |     """
 846 |     if not _isconvertible(float, string):
 847 |         return False
 848 |     elif isinstance(string, (str, bytes)) and (
 849 |         math.isinf(float(string)) or math.isnan(float(string))
 850 |     ):
 851 |         return string.lower() in ["inf", "-inf", "nan"]
 852 |     return True

 859 |     >>> _isint("123.45")
 860 |     False
 861 |     """
 862 |     return (
 863 |         type(string) is inttype
 864 |         or isinstance(string, (bytes, str))

 873 |     >>> _isbool("False")
 874 |     True
 875 |     >>> _isbool(1)
 876 |     False

 883 | def _type(string, has_invisible=True, numparse=True):
 884 |     """The least generic type (type(None), int, float, str, unicode).
 885 | 
 886 |     >>> _type(None) is type(None)
 887 |     True
 888 |     >>> _type("foo") is type("")
 889 |     True
 890 |     >>> _type("1") is type(1)
 891 |     True
 892 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 893 |     True
 894 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 895 |     True
 896 | 
 897 |     """
 898 | 
 899 |     if has_invisible and isinstance(string, (str, bytes)):
 900 |         string = _strip_ansi(string)
 901 | 
 902 |     if string is None:
 903 |         return type(None)
 904 |     elif hasattr(string, "isoformat"):  # datetime.datetime, date, and time
 905 |         return str
 906 |     elif _isbool(string):
 907 |         return bool
 908 |     elif _isint(string) and numparse:
 909 |         return int
 910 |     elif _isnumber(string) and numparse:
 911 |         return float
 912 |     elif isinstance(string, bytes):
 913 |         return bytes
 914 |     else:
 915 |         return str

 918 | def _afterpoint(string):
 919 |     """Symbols after a decimal point, -1 if the string lacks the decimal point.
 920 | 
 921 |     >>> _afterpoint("123.45")
 922 |     2
 923 |     >>> _afterpoint("1001")
 924 |     -1
 925 |     >>> _afterpoint("eggs")
 926 |     -1
 927 |     >>> _afterpoint("123e45")
 928 |     2
 929 |     >>> _afterpoint("123,456.78")
 930 |     2
 931 | 
 932 |     """
 933 |     if _isnumber(string) or _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 934 |         if _isint(string):
 935 |             return -1
 936 |         else:
 937 |             pos = string.rfind(".")
 938 |             pos = string.lower().rfind("e") if pos < 0 else pos
 939 |             if pos >= 0:
 940 |                 return len(string) - pos - 1
 941 |             else:
 942 |                 return -1  # no point
 943 |     else:
 944 |         return -1  # not a number

1546 |     >>> repr(_to_str(42))
1547 |     "'42'"
1548 | 
1549 |     """
1550 |     if isinstance(s, bytes):
1551 |         return s.decode(encoding=encoding, errors=errors)
1552 |     return str(s)

1555 | def tabulate(
1556 |     tabular_data,
1557 |     headers=(),
1558 |     tablefmt="simple",
1559 |     floatfmt=_DEFAULT_FLOATFMT,
1560 |     intfmt=_DEFAULT_INTFMT,
1561 |     numalign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1562 |     stralign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1563 |     missingval=_DEFAULT_MISSINGVAL,
1564 |     showindex="default",
1565 |     disable_numparse=False,
1566 |     colalign=None,
1567 |     maxcolwidths=None,
1568 |     rowalign=None,
1569 |     maxheadercolwidths=None,
1570 | ):
1571 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1572 | 
1573 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1574 |     ---  ---------
1575 |       1      2.34
1576 |     -56      8.999
1577 |       2  10001
1578 |     ---  ---------
1579 | 
1580 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1581 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1582 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1583 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1584 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1585 | 
1586 | 
1587 |     Table headers
1588 |     -------------
1589 | 
1590 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1591 | 
1592 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1593 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1594 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1595 | 
1596 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1597 | 
1598 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1599 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1600 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1601 | 
1602 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1603 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1604 |            sex      age
1605 |     -----  -----  -----
1606 |     Alice  F         24
1607 |     Bob    M         19
1608 | 
1609 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1610 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1611 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1612 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1613 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1614 | 
1615 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1616 |     -  -  --
1617 |     0  F  24
1618 |     1  M  19
1619 |     -  -  --
1620 | 
1621 | 
1622 |     Column alignment
1623 |     ----------------
1624 | 
1625 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1626 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1627 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1628 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1629 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1630 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1631 | 
1632 | 
1633 |     Table formats
1634 |     -------------
1635 | 
1636 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1637 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1638 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1639 | 
1640 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1641 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1642 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1643 | 
1644 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1645 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1646 |     columns):
1647 | 
1648 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1649 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1650 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1651 |     -----  --  ----
1652 |     spam    1  ?
1653 |     eggs   42  3.14
1654 |     other   ?  2.7
1655 |     -----  --  ----
1656 | 
1657 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:
1658 |     'plain', 'simple', 'grid', 'pipe', 'orgtbl', 'rst', 'mediawiki',
1659 |     'latex', 'latex_raw', 'latex_booktabs', 'latex_longtable' and tsv.
1660 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.
1661 | 
1662 |     "plain" format doesn't use any pseudographics to draw tables,
1663 |     it separates columns with a double space:
1664 | 
1665 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1666 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "plain"))

1669 |     eggs        451

2007 |     Number parsing
2008 |     --------------
2009 |     By default, anything which can be parsed as a number is a number.
2010 |     This ensures numbers represented as strings are aligned properly.
2011 |     This can lead to weird results for particular strings such as
2012 |     specific git SHAs e.g. "42992e1" will be parsed into the number
2013 |     429920 and aligned as such.
2014 | 
2015 |     To completely disable number parsing (and alignment), use
2016 |     `disable_numparse=True`. For more fine grained control, a list column
2017 |     indices is used to disable number parsing only on those columns
2018 |     e.g. `disable_numparse=[0, 2]` would disable number parsing only on the
2019 |     first and third columns.
2020 | 
2021 |     Column Widths and Auto Line Wrapping
2022 |     ------------------------------------
2023 |     Tabulate will, by default, set the width of each column to the length of the
2024 |     longest element in that column. However, in situations where fields are expected
2025 |     to reasonably be too long to look good as a single line, tabulate can help automate
2026 |     word wrapping long fields for you. Use the parameter `maxcolwidth` to provide a
2027 |     list of maximal column widths
2028 | 
2029 |     >>> print(tabulate( \
2030 |           [('1', 'John Smith', \
2031 |             'This is a rather long description that might look better if it is wrapped a bit')], \
2032 |           headers=("Issue Id", "Author", "Description"), \
2033 |           maxcolwidths=[None, None, 30], \
2034 |           tablefmt="grid"  \
2035 |         ))
2036 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2037 |     |   Issue Id | Author     | Description                   |
2038 |     +============+============+===============================+
2039 |     |          1 | John Smith | This is a rather long         |
2040 |     |            |            | description that might look   |
2041 |     |            |            | better if it is wrapped a bit |
2042 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2043 | 
2044 |     Header column width can be specified in a similar way using `maxheadercolwidth`
2045 | 
2046 |     """
2047 | 
2048 |     if tabular_data is None:
2049 |         tabular_data = []
2050 | 
2051 |     list_of_lists, headers = _normalize_tabular_data(
2052 |         tabular_data, headers, showindex=showindex
2053 |     )
2054 |     list_of_lists, separating_lines = _remove_separating_lines(list_of_lists)
2055 |

 717 | # Handle ANSI escape sequences for both control sequence introducer (CSI) and
 718 | # operating system command (OSC). Both of these begin with 0x1b (or octal 033),
 719 | # which will be shown below as ESC.
 720 | #
 721 | # CSI ANSI escape codes have the following format, defined in section 5.4 of ECMA-48:
 722 | #
 723 | # CSI: ESC followed by the '[' character (0x5b)
 724 | # Parameter Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x30-0x3f
 725 | # Intermediate Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x20-0x2f
 726 | # Final Byte: a single byte in the range 0x40-0x7e
 727 | #
 728 | # Also include the terminal hyperlink sequences as described here:
 729 | # https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda
 730 | #
 731 | # OSC 8 ; params ; uri ST display_text OSC 8 ;; ST
 732 | #
 733 | # Example: \x1b]8;;https://example.com\x5ctext to show\x1b]8;;\x5c
 734 | #
 735 | # Where:
 736 | # OSC: ESC followed by the ']' character (0x5d)
 737 | # params: 0..n optional key value pairs separated by ':' (e.g. foo=bar:baz=qux:abc=123)
 738 | # URI: the actual URI with protocol scheme (e.g. https://, file://, ftp://)
 739 | # ST: ESC followed by the '\' character (0x5c)
 740 | _esc = r"\x1b"
 741 | _csi = rf"{_esc}\["
 742 | _osc = rf"{_esc}\]"
 743 | _st = rf"{_esc}\\"
 744 | 
 745 | _ansi_escape_pat = rf"""
 746 |     (
 747 |         # terminal colors, etc
 748 |         {_csi}        # CSI
 749 |         [\x30-\x3f]*  # parameter bytes
 750 |         [\x20-\x2f]*  # intermediate bytes
 751 |         [\x40-\x7e]   # final byte
 752 |     |
 753 |         # terminal hyperlinks
 754 |         {_osc}8;        # OSC opening
 755 |         (\w+=\w+:?)*    # key=value params list (submatch 2)
 756 |         ;               # delimiter
 757 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # URI - anything but ESC (submatch 3)
 758 |         {_st}           # ST
 759 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # link text - anything but ESC (submatch 4)
 760 |         {_osc}8;;{_st}  # "closing" OSC sequence
 761 |     )
 762 | """
 763 | _ansi_codes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat, re.VERBOSE)
 764 | _ansi_codes_bytes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat.encode("utf8"), re.VERBOSE)

 792 | def _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 793 |     """
 794 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".")
 795 |     False
 796 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1")
 797 |     True
 798 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1.")
 799 |     True
 800 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".1")
 801 |     True
 802 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1000")
 803 |     False
 804 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000")
 805 |     True
 806 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,0000")
 807 |     False
 808 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000.1234")
 809 |     True
 810 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(b"1,000.1234")
 811 |     True
 812 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("+1,000.1234")
 813 |     True
 814 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("-1,000.1234")
 815 |     True
 816 |     """
 817 |     try:
 818 |         string = string.decode()
 819 |     except (UnicodeDecodeError, AttributeError):
 820 |         pass
 821 | 
 822 |     return bool(re.match(_float_with_thousands_separators, string))

 833 | def _isnumber(string):
 834 |     """
 835 |     >>> _isnumber("123.45")
 836 |     True
 837 |     >>> _isnumber("123")
 838 |     True
 839 |     >>> _isnumber("spam")
 840 |     False
 841 |     >>> _isnumber("123e45678")
 842 |     False
 843 |     >>> _isnumber("inf")
 844 |     True
 845 |     """
 846 |     if not _isconvertible(float, string):
 847 |         return False
 848 |     elif isinstance(string, (str, bytes)) and (
 849 |         math.isinf(float(string)) or math.isnan(float(string))
 850 |     ):
 851 |         return string.lower() in ["inf", "-inf", "nan"]
 852 |     return True

 883 | def _type(string, has_invisible=True, numparse=True):
 884 |     """The least generic type (type(None), int, float, str, unicode).
 885 | 
 886 |     >>> _type(None) is type(None)
 887 |     True

 889 |     True
 890 |     >>> _type("1") is type(1)
 891 |     True
 892 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 893 |     True
 894 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 895 |     True
 896 | 
 897 |     """
 898 | 
 899 |     if has_invisible and isinstance(string, (str, bytes)):
 900 |         string = _strip_ansi(string)
 901 | 
 902 |     if string is None:
 903 |         return type(None)
 904 |     elif hasattr(string, "isoformat"):  # datetime.datetime, date, and time
 905 |         return str
 906 |     elif _isbool(string):
 907 |         return bool
 908 |     elif _isint(string) and numparse:
 909 |         return int
 910 |     elif _isnumber(string) and numparse:
 911 |         return float
 912 |     elif isinstance(string, bytes):

 914 |     else:

 918 | def _afterpoint(string):
 919 |     """Symbols after a decimal point, -1 if the string lacks the decimal point.
 920 | 
 921 |     >>> _afterpoint("123.45")
 922 |     2
 923 |     >>> _afterpoint("1001")
 924 |     -1
 925 |     >>> _afterpoint("eggs")
 926 |     -1
 927 |     >>> _afterpoint("123e45")
 928 |     2
 929 |     >>> _afterpoint("123,456.78")
 930 |     2
 931 | 
 932 |     """
 933 |     if _isnumber(string) or _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 934 |         if _isint(string):
 935 |             return -1
 936 |         else:
 937 |             pos = string.rfind(".")
 938 |             pos = string.lower().rfind("e") if pos < 0 else pos
 939 |             if pos >= 0:
 940 |                 return len(string) - pos - 1
 941 |             else:
 942 |                 return -1  # no point
 943 |     else:
 944 |         return -1  # not a number

1560 |     floatfmt=_DEFAULT_FLOATFMT,
1561 |     intfmt=_DEFAULT_INTFMT,
1562 |     numalign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1563 |     stralign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1564 |     missingval=_DEFAULT_MISSINGVAL,

1566 |     disable_numparse=False,

1572 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1573 | 
1574 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1575 |     ---  ---------
1576 |       1      2.34
1577 |     -56      8.999
1578 |       2  10001
1579 |     ---  ---------
1580 | 
1581 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1582 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1583 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1584 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1585 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1586 | 
1587 | 
1588 |     Table headers
1589 |     -------------
1590 | 
1591 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1592 | 
1593 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1594 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1595 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1596 | 
1597 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1598 | 
1599 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1600 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1601 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1602 | 
1603 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1604 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1605 |            sex      age
1606 |     -----  -----  -----
1607 |     Alice  F         24
1608 |     Bob    M         19
1609 | 
1610 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1611 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1612 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1613 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1614 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1615 | 
1616 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1617 |     -  -  --
1618 |     0  F  24
1619 |     1  M  19
1620 |     -  -  --
1621 | 
1622 | 
1623 |     Column alignment
1624 |     ----------------
1625 | 
1626 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1627 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1628 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1629 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1630 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1631 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1632 |

1634 |     Table formats
1635 |     -------------
1636 | 
1637 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1638 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1639 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1640 | 
1641 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1642 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1643 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.

1646 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different

2008 |     Number parsing
2009 |     --------------
2010 |     By default, anything which can be parsed as a number is a number.
2011 |     This ensures numbers represented as strings are aligned properly.
2012 |     This can lead to weird results for particular strings such as
2013 |     specific git SHAs e.g. "42992e1" will be parsed into the number
2014 |     429920 and aligned as such.
2015 | 
2016 |     To completely disable number parsing (and alignment), use
2017 |     `disable_numparse=True`. For more fine grained control, a list column
2018 |     indices is used to disable number parsing only on those columns
2019 |     e.g. `disable_numparse=[0, 2]` would disable number parsing only on the
2020 |     first and third columns.
2021 | 
2022 |     Column Widths and Auto Line Wrapping
2023 |     ------------------------------------
2024 |     Tabulate will, by default, set the width of each column to the length of the
2025 |     longest element in that column. However, in situations where fields are expected
2026 |     to reasonably be too long to look good as a single line, tabulate can help automate
2027 |     word wrapping long fields for you. Use the parameter `maxcolwidth` to provide a
2028 |     list of maximal column widths
2029 | 
2030 |     >>> print(tabulate( \
2031 |           [('1', 'John Smith', \
2032 |             'This is a rather long description that might look better if it is wrapped a bit')], \
2033 |           headers=("Issue Id", "Author", "Description"), \
2034 |           maxcolwidths=[None, None, 30], \
2035 |           tablefmt="grid"  \
2036 |         ))
2037 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2038 |     |   Issue Id | Author     | Description                   |
2039 |     +============+============+===============================+
2040 |     |          1 | John Smith | This is a rather long         |
2041 |     |            |            | description that might look   |
2042 |     |            |            | better if it is wrapped a bit |
2043 |     +------------+------------+-------------------------------+
2044 | 
2045 |     Header column width can be specified in a similar way using `maxheadercolwidth`
2046 | 
2047 |     """
2048 | 
2049 |     if tabular_data is None:
2050 |         tabular_data = []
2051 | 
2052 |     list_of_lists, headers = _normalize_tabular_data(
2053 |         tabular_data, headers, showindex=showindex
2054 |     )
2055 |     list_of_lists, separating_lines = _remove_separating_lines(list_of_lists)
2056 | 
2057 |     if maxcolwidths is not None:
2058 |         num_cols = len(list_of_lists[0])
2059 |         if isinstance(maxcolwidths, int):  # Expand scalar for all columns
2060 |             maxcolwidths = _expand_iterable(maxcolwidths, num_cols, maxcolwidths)
2061 |         else:  # Ignore col width for any 'trailing' columns
2062 |             maxcolwidths = _expand_iterable(maxcolwidths, num_cols, None)

 717 | # Handle ANSI escape sequences for both control sequence introducer (CSI) and
 718 | # operating system command (OSC). Both of these begin with 0x1b (or octal 033),
 719 | # which will be shown below as ESC.
 720 | #
 721 | # CSI ANSI escape codes have the following format, defined in section 5.4 of ECMA-48:
 722 | #
 723 | # CSI: ESC followed by the '[' character (0x5b)
 724 | # Parameter Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x30-0x3f
 725 | # Intermediate Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x20-0x2f
 726 | # Final Byte: a single byte in the range 0x40-0x7e
 727 | #
 728 | # Also include the terminal hyperlink sequences as described here:
 729 | # https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda
 730 | #
 731 | # OSC 8 ; params ; uri ST display_text OSC 8 ;; ST
 732 | #
 733 | # Example: \x1b]8;;https://example.com\x5ctext to show\x1b]8;;\x5c
 734 | #
 735 | # Where:
 736 | # OSC: ESC followed by the ']' character (0x5d)
 737 | # params: 0..n optional key value pairs separated by ':' (e.g. foo=bar:baz=qux:abc=123)
 738 | # URI: the actual URI with protocol scheme (e.g. https://, file://, ftp://)
 739 | # ST: ESC followed by the '\' character (0x5c)
 740 | _esc = r"\x1b"
 741 | _csi = rf"{_esc}\["
 742 | _osc = rf"{_esc}\]"
 743 | _st = rf"{_esc}\\"
 744 | 
 745 | _ansi_escape_pat = rf"""
 746 |     (
 747 |         # terminal colors, etc
 748 |         {_csi}        # CSI
 749 |         [\x30-\x3f]*  # parameter bytes
 750 |         [\x20-\x2f]*  # intermediate bytes
 751 |         [\x40-\x7e]   # final byte
 752 |     |
 753 |         # terminal hyperlinks
 754 |         {_osc}8;        # OSC opening
 755 |         (\w+=\w+:?)*    # key=value params list (submatch 2)
 756 |         ;               # delimiter
 757 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # URI - anything but ESC (submatch 3)
 758 |         {_st}           # ST
 759 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # link text - anything but ESC (submatch 4)
 760 |         {_osc}8;;{_st}  # "closing" OSC sequence
 761 |     )
 762 | """
 763 | _ansi_codes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat, re.VERBOSE)
 764 | _ansi_codes_bytes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat.encode("utf8"), re.VERBOSE)
 765 | _ansi_color_reset_code = "\033[0m"

 792 | def _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 793 |     """
 794 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".")
 795 |     False
 796 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1")
 797 |     True
 798 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1.")
 799 |     True
 800 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".1")
 801 |     True
 802 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1000")
 803 |     False
 804 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000")
 805 |     True
 806 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,0000")
 807 |     False
 808 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000.1234")
 809 |     True
 810 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(b"1,000.1234")
 811 |     True
 812 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("+1,000.1234")
 813 |     True
 814 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("-1,000.1234")
 815 |     True
 816 |     """
 817 |     try:
 818 |         string = string.decode()
 819 |     except (UnicodeDecodeError, AttributeError):
 820 |         pass
 821 | 
 822 |     return bool(re.match(_float_with_thousands_separators, string))

 833 | def _isnumber(string):
 834 |     """
 835 |     >>> _isnumber("123.45")
 836 |     True
 837 |     >>> _isnumber("123")
 838 |     True
 839 |     >>> _isnumber("spam")
 840 |     False
 841 |     >>> _isnumber("123e45678")
 842 |     False
 843 |     >>> _isnumber("inf")
 844 |     True
 845 |     """
 846 |     if not _isconvertible(float, string):
 847 |         return False
 848 |     elif isinstance(string, (str, bytes)) and (
 849 |         math.isinf(float(string)) or math.isnan(float(string))
 850 |     ):
 851 |         return string.lower() in ["inf", "-inf", "nan"]
 852 |     return True

 858 |     True
 859 |     >>> _isint("123.45")
 860 |     False
 861 |     """
 862 |     return (
 863 |         type(string) is inttype
 864 |         or isinstance(string, (bytes, str))
 865 |         and _isconvertible(inttype, string)

 869 | def _isbool(string):
 870 |     """
 871 |     >>> _isbool(True)
 872 |     True
 873 |     >>> _isbool("False")
 874 |     True
 875 |     >>> _isbool(1)
 876 |     False
 877 |     """
 878 |     return type(string) is bool or (
 879 |         isinstance(string, (bytes, str)) and string in ("True", "False")

 883 | def _type(string, has_invisible=True, numparse=True):
 884 |     """The least generic type (type(None), int, float, str, unicode).
 885 | 
 886 |     >>> _type(None) is type(None)
 887 |     True
 888 |     >>> _type("foo") is type("")
 889 |     True
 890 |     >>> _type("1") is type(1)
 891 |     True
 892 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 893 |     True
 894 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 895 |     True
 896 | 
 897 |     """
 898 | 
 899 |     if has_invisible and isinstance(string, (str, bytes)):
 900 |         string = _strip_ansi(string)
 901 | 
 902 |     if string is None:
 903 |         return type(None)
 904 |     elif hasattr(string, "isoformat"):  # datetime.datetime, date, and time
 905 |         return str
 906 |     elif _isbool(string):
 907 |         return bool

1486 |         if index is None:
1487 |             index = list(range(len(rows)))
1488 |         rows = _prepend_row_index(rows, index)
1489 |     elif showindex == "never" or (not _bool(showindex) and not showindex_is_a_str):
1490 |         pass
1491 | 
1492 |     # pad with empty headers for initial columns if necessary
1493 |     if headers and len(rows) > 0:
1494 |         nhs = len(headers)
1495 |         ncols = len(rows[0])
1496 |         if nhs < ncols:
1497 |             headers = [""] * (ncols - nhs) + headers
1498 | 
1499 |     return rows, headers

1502 | def _wrap_text_to_colwidths(list_of_lists, colwidths, numparses=True):
1503 |     numparses = _expand_iterable(numparses, len(list_of_lists[0]), True)
1504 | 
1505 |     result = []
1506 | 
1507 |     for row in list_of_lists:
1508 |         new_row = []
1509 |         for cell, width, numparse in zip(row, colwidths, numparses):
1510 |             if _isnumber(cell) and numparse:
1511 |                 new_row.append(cell)
1512 |                 continue
1513 | 
1514 |             if width is not None:
1515 |                 wrapper = _CustomTextWrap(width=width)
1516 |                 # Cast based on our internal type handling
1517 |                 # Any future custom formatting of types (such as datetimes)
1518 |                 # may need to be more explicit than just `str` of the object
1519 |                 casted_cell = (
1520 |                     str(cell) if _isnumber(cell) else _type(cell, numparse)(cell)
1521 |                 )
1522 |                 wrapped = wrapper.wrap(casted_cell)
1523 |                 new_row.append("\n".join(wrapped))
1524 |             else:
1525 |                 new_row.append(cell)
1526 |         result.append(new_row)
1527 | 
1528 |     return result

1531 | def _to_str(s, encoding="utf8", errors="ignore"):
1532 |     """
1533 |     A type safe wrapper for converting a bytestring to str. This is essentially just
1534 |     a wrapper around .decode() intended for use with things like map(), but with some
1535 |     specific behavior:
1536 | 
1537 |     1. if the given parameter is not a bytestring, it is returned unmodified
1538 |     2. decode() is called for the given parameter and assumes utf8 encoding, but the
1539 |        default error behavior is changed from 'strict' to 'ignore'
1540 | 
1541 |     >>> repr(_to_str(b'foo'))
1542 |     "'foo'"
1543 | 
1544 |     >>> repr(_to_str('foo'))
1545 |     "'foo'"
1546 | 
1547 |     >>> repr(_to_str(42))
1548 |     "'42'"
1549 | 
1550 |     """
1551 |     if isinstance(s, bytes):
1552 |         return s.decode(encoding=encoding, errors=errors)
1553 |     return str(s)

1556 | def tabulate(
1557 |     tabular_data,
1558 |     headers=(),
1559 |     tablefmt="simple",
1560 |     floatfmt=_DEFAULT_FLOATFMT,
1561 |     intfmt=_DEFAULT_INTFMT,
1562 |     numalign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1563 |     stralign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1564 |     missingval=_DEFAULT_MISSINGVAL,
1565 |     showindex="default",
1566 |     disable_numparse=False,
1567 |     colalign=None,
1568 |     maxcolwidths=None,
1569 |     rowalign=None,
1570 |     maxheadercolwidths=None,
1571 | ):
1572 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1573 | 
1574 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1575 |     ---  ---------
1576 |       1      2.34
1577 |     -56      8.999
1578 |       2  10001
1579 |     ---  ---------
1580 | 
1581 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1582 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1583 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1584 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1585 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1586 | 
1587 | 
1588 |     Table headers
1589 |     -------------
1590 | 
1591 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1592 | 
1593 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1594 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1595 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1596 | 
1597 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1598 | 
1599 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1600 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1601 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1602 | 
1603 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1604 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1605 |            sex      age
1606 |     -----  -----  -----
1607 |     Alice  F         24
1608 |     Bob    M         19
1609 | 
1610 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1611 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1612 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1613 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1614 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1615 | 
1616 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1617 |     -  -  --
1618 |     0  F  24
1619 |     1  M  19
1620 |     -  -  --
1621 | 
1622 | 
1623 |     Column alignment
1624 |     ----------------
1625 | 
1626 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1627 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1628 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1629 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1630 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1631 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1632 | 
1633 | 
1634 |     Table formats
1635 |     -------------
1636 | 
1637 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1638 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1639 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1640 | 
1641 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1642 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1643 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1644 | 
1645 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1646 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1647 |     columns):
1648 | 
1649 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1650 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1651 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1652 |     -----  --  ----
1653 |     spam    1  ?
1654 |     eggs   42  3.14
1655 |     other   ?  2.7
1656 |     -----  --  ----
1657 | 
1658 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:
1659 |     'plain', 'simple', 'grid', 'pipe', 'orgtbl', 'rst', 'mediawiki',
1660 |     'latex', 'latex_raw', 'latex_booktabs', 'latex_longtable' and tsv.
1661 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.
1662 | 
1663 |     "plain" format doesn't use any pseudographics to draw tables,
1664 |     it separates columns with a double space:
1665 | 
1666 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1667 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "plain"))
1668 |     strings      numbers
1669 |     spam         41.9999
1670 |     eggs        451
1671 | 
1672 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]], tablefmt="plain"))
1673 |     spam   41.9999
1674 |     eggs  451
1675 | 
1676 |     "simple" format is like Pandoc simple_tables:
1677 | 
1678 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1679 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "simple"))

1681 |     ---------  ---------
1682 |     spam         41.9999
1683 |     eggs        451
1684 | 
1685 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]], tablefmt="simple"))
1686 |     ----  --------
1687 |     spam   41.9999

 717 | # Handle ANSI escape sequences for both control sequence introducer (CSI) and
 718 | # operating system command (OSC). Both of these begin with 0x1b (or octal 033),
 719 | # which will be shown below as ESC.
 720 | #
 721 | # CSI ANSI escape codes have the following format, defined in section 5.4 of ECMA-48:
 722 | #
 723 | # CSI: ESC followed by the '[' character (0x5b)
 724 | # Parameter Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x30-0x3f
 725 | # Intermediate Bytes: 0..n bytes in the range 0x20-0x2f
 726 | # Final Byte: a single byte in the range 0x40-0x7e
 727 | #
 728 | # Also include the terminal hyperlink sequences as described here:
 729 | # https://gist.github.com/egmontkob/eb114294efbcd5adb1944c9f3cb5feda
 730 | #
 731 | # OSC 8 ; params ; uri ST display_text OSC 8 ;; ST
 732 | #
 733 | # Example: \x1b]8;;https://example.com\x5ctext to show\x1b]8;;\x5c
 734 | #
 735 | # Where:
 736 | # OSC: ESC followed by the ']' character (0x5d)
 737 | # params: 0..n optional key value pairs separated by ':' (e.g. foo=bar:baz=qux:abc=123)
 738 | # URI: the actual URI with protocol scheme (e.g. https://, file://, ftp://)
 739 | # ST: ESC followed by the '\' character (0x5c)
 740 | _esc = r"\x1b"
 741 | _csi = rf"{_esc}\["
 742 | _osc = rf"{_esc}\]"
 743 | _st = rf"{_esc}\\"
 744 | 
 745 | _ansi_escape_pat = rf"""
 746 |     (
 747 |         # terminal colors, etc
 748 |         {_csi}        # CSI
 749 |         [\x30-\x3f]*  # parameter bytes
 750 |         [\x20-\x2f]*  # intermediate bytes
 751 |         [\x40-\x7e]   # final byte
 752 |     |
 753 |         # terminal hyperlinks
 754 |         {_osc}8;        # OSC opening
 755 |         (\w+=\w+:?)*    # key=value params list (submatch 2)
 756 |         ;               # delimiter
 757 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # URI - anything but ESC (submatch 3)
 758 |         {_st}           # ST
 759 |         ([^{_esc}]+)    # link text - anything but ESC (submatch 4)
 760 |         {_osc}8;;{_st}  # "closing" OSC sequence
 761 |     )
 762 | """
 763 | _ansi_codes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat, re.VERBOSE)
 764 | _ansi_codes_bytes = re.compile(_ansi_escape_pat.encode("utf8"), re.VERBOSE)

 792 | def _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(string):
 793 |     """
 794 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".")
 795 |     False
 796 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1")
 797 |     True
 798 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1.")
 799 |     True
 800 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(".1")
 801 |     True
 802 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1000")
 803 |     False
 804 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000")
 805 |     True
 806 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,0000")
 807 |     False
 808 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("1,000.1234")
 809 |     True
 810 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator(b"1,000.1234")
 811 |     True
 812 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("+1,000.1234")
 813 |     True
 814 |     >>> _isnumber_with_thousands_separator("-1,000.1234")
 815 |     True
 816 |     """
 817 |     try:
 818 |         string = string.decode()
 819 |     except (UnicodeDecodeError, AttributeError):
 820 |         pass
 821 | 
 822 |     return bool(re.match(_float_with_thousands_separators, string))

 833 | def _isnumber(string):
 834 |     """
 835 |     >>> _isnumber("123.45")
 836 |     True
 837 |     >>> _isnumber("123")
 838 |     True
 839 |     >>> _isnumber("spam")
 840 |     False
 841 |     >>> _isnumber("123e45678")
 842 |     False
 843 |     >>> _isnumber("inf")
 844 |     True
 845 |     """
 846 |     if not _isconvertible(float, string):
 847 |         return False
 848 |     elif isinstance(string, (str, bytes)) and (
 849 |         math.isinf(float(string)) or math.isnan(float(string))
 850 |     ):
 851 |         return string.lower() in ["inf", "-inf", "nan"]
 852 |     return True

 883 | def _type(string, has_invisible=True, numparse=True):
 884 |     """The least generic type (type(None), int, float, str, unicode).
 885 | 
 886 |     >>> _type(None) is type(None)
 887 |     True

 889 |     True
 890 |     >>> _type("1") is type(1)
 891 |     True
 892 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 893 |     True
 894 |     >>> _type('\x1b[31m42\x1b[0m') is type(42)
 895 |     True
 896 | 
 897 |     """
 898 | 
 899 |     if has_invisible and isinstance(string, (str, bytes)):
 900 |         string = _strip_ansi(string)

 903 |         return type(None)
 904 |     elif hasattr(string, "isoformat"):  # datetime.datetime, date, and time
 905 |         return str
 906 |     elif _isbool(string):

 908 |     elif _isint(string) and numparse:
 909 |         return int
 910 |     elif _isnumber(string) and numparse:
 911 |         return float

1499 |     numparses = _expand_iterable(numparses, len(list_of_lists[0]), True)
1500 | 
1501 |     result = []
1502 | 
1503 |     for row in list_of_lists:
1504 |         new_row = []
1505 |         for cell, width, numparse in zip(row, colwidths, numparses):
1506 |             if _isnumber(cell) and numparse:
1507 |                 new_row.append(cell)
1508 |                 continue
1509 | 
1510 |             if width is not None:
1511 |                 wrapper = _CustomTextWrap(width=width)
1512 |                 # Cast based on our internal type handling
1513 |                 # Any future custom formatting of types (such as datetimes)
1514 |                 # may need to be more explicit than just `str` of the object
1515 |                 casted_cell = (
1516 |                     str(cell) if _isnumber(cell) else _type(cell, numparse)(cell)
1517 |                 )
1518 |                 wrapped = wrapper.wrap(casted_cell)
1519 |                 new_row.append("\n".join(wrapped))
1520 |             else:
1521 |                 new_row.append(cell)
1522 |         result.append(new_row)
1523 | 
1524 |     return result

1527 | def _to_str(s, encoding="utf8", errors="ignore"):
1528 |     """
1529 |     A type safe wrapper for converting a bytestring to str. This is essentially just
1530 |     a wrapper around .decode() intended for use with things like map(), but with some
1531 |     specific behavior:
1532 | 
1533 |     1. if the given parameter is not a bytestring, it is returned unmodified
1534 |     2. decode() is called for the given parameter and assumes utf8 encoding, but the
1535 |        default error behavior is changed from 'strict' to 'ignore'
1536 | 
1537 |     >>> repr(_to_str(b'foo'))
1538 |     "'foo'"
1539 | 
1540 |     >>> repr(_to_str('foo'))
1541 |     "'foo'"
1542 | 
1543 |     >>> repr(_to_str(42))
1544 |     "'42'"
1545 | 
1546 |     """
1547 |     if isinstance(s, bytes):
1548 |         return s.decode(encoding=encoding, errors=errors)
1549 |     return str(s)

1552 | def tabulate(
1553 |     tabular_data,
1554 |     headers=(),
1555 |     tablefmt="simple",
1556 |     floatfmt=_DEFAULT_FLOATFMT,
1557 |     intfmt=_DEFAULT_INTFMT,
1558 |     numalign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1559 |     stralign=_DEFAULT_ALIGN,
1560 |     missingval=_DEFAULT_MISSINGVAL,
1561 |     showindex="default",
1562 |     disable_numparse=False,
1563 |     colalign=None,
1564 |     maxcolwidths=None,
1565 |     rowalign=None,
1566 |     maxheadercolwidths=None,
1567 | ):
1568 |     """Format a fixed width table for pretty printing.
1569 | 
1570 |     >>> print(tabulate([[1, 2.34], [-56, "8.999"], ["2", "10001"]]))
1571 |     ---  ---------
1572 |       1      2.34
1573 |     -56      8.999
1574 |       2  10001
1575 |     ---  ---------
1576 | 
1577 |     The first required argument (`tabular_data`) can be a
1578 |     list-of-lists (or another iterable of iterables), a list of named
1579 |     tuples, a dictionary of iterables, an iterable of dictionaries,
1580 |     an iterable of dataclasses (Python 3.7+), a two-dimensional NumPy array,
1581 |     NumPy record array, or a Pandas' dataframe.
1582 | 
1583 | 
1584 |     Table headers
1585 |     -------------
1586 | 
1587 |     To print nice column headers, supply the second argument (`headers`):
1588 | 
1589 |       - `headers` can be an explicit list of column headers
1590 |       - if `headers="firstrow"`, then the first row of data is used
1591 |       - if `headers="keys"`, then dictionary keys or column indices are used
1592 | 
1593 |     Otherwise a headerless table is produced.
1594 | 
1595 |     If the number of headers is less than the number of columns, they
1596 |     are supposed to be names of the last columns. This is consistent
1597 |     with the plain-text format of R and Pandas' dataframes.
1598 | 
1599 |     >>> print(tabulate([["sex","age"],["Alice","F",24],["Bob","M",19]],
1600 |     ...       headers="firstrow"))
1601 |            sex      age
1602 |     -----  -----  -----
1603 |     Alice  F         24
1604 |     Bob    M         19
1605 | 
1606 |     By default, pandas.DataFrame data have an additional column called
1607 |     row index. To add a similar column to all other types of data,
1608 |     use `showindex="always"` or `showindex=True`. To suppress row indices
1609 |     for all types of data, pass `showindex="never" or `showindex=False`.
1610 |     To add a custom row index column, pass `showindex=some_iterable`.
1611 | 
1612 |     >>> print(tabulate([["F",24],["M",19]], showindex="always"))
1613 |     -  -  --
1614 |     0  F  24
1615 |     1  M  19
1616 |     -  -  --
1617 | 
1618 | 
1619 |     Column alignment
1620 |     ----------------
1621 | 
1622 |     `tabulate` tries to detect column types automatically, and aligns
1623 |     the values properly. By default it aligns decimal points of the
1624 |     numbers (or flushes integer numbers to the right), and flushes
1625 |     everything else to the left. Possible column alignments
1626 |     (`numalign`, `stralign`) are: "right", "center", "left", "decimal"
1627 |     (only for `numalign`), and None (to disable alignment).
1628 | 
1629 | 
1630 |     Table formats
1631 |     -------------
1632 | 
1633 |     `intfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1634 |     contain numeric data without a decimal point. This can also be
1635 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1636 | 
1637 |     `floatfmt` is a format specification used for columns which
1638 |     contain numeric data with a decimal point. This can also be
1639 |     a list or tuple of format strings, one per column.
1640 | 
1641 |     `None` values are replaced with a `missingval` string (like
1642 |     `floatfmt`, this can also be a list of values for different
1643 |     columns):
1644 | 
1645 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 1, None],
1646 |     ...                 ["eggs", 42, 3.14],
1647 |     ...                 ["other", None, 2.7]], missingval="?"))
1648 |     -----  --  ----
1649 |     spam    1  ?
1650 |     eggs   42  3.14
1651 |     other   ?  2.7
1652 |     -----  --  ----
1653 | 
1654 |     Various plain-text table formats (`tablefmt`) are supported:
1655 |     'plain', 'simple', 'grid', 'pipe', 'orgtbl', 'rst', 'mediawiki',
1656 |     'latex', 'latex_raw', 'latex_booktabs', 'latex_longtable' and tsv.
1657 |     Variable `tabulate_formats`contains the list of currently supported formats.
1658 | 
1659 |     "plain" format doesn't use any pseudographics to draw tables,
1660 |     it separates columns with a double space:
1661 | 
1662 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]],
1663 |     ...                 ["strings", "numbers"], "plain"))
1664 |     strings      numbers
1665 |     spam         41.9999
1666 |     eggs        451
1667 | 
1668 |     >>> print(tabulate([["spam", 41.9999], ["eggs", "451.0"]], tablefmt="plain"))

2004 |     Number parsing
2005 |     --------------
2006 |     By default, anything which can be parsed as a number is a number.
2007 |     This ensures numbers represented as strings are aligned properly.
2008 |     This can lead to weird results for particular strings such as
2009 |     specific git SHAs e.g. "42992e1" will be parsed into the number
2010 |     429920 and aligned as such.
2011 | 
2012 |     To completely disable number parsing (and alignment), use
2013 |     `disable_numparse=True`. For more fine grained control, a list column
